newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans to revisit tough budget issues.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans to revisit tough budget issues.

text.p: President Clinton meets congressional Republican leaders Tuesday, confident they can cross party lines and carry out a voter mandate to balance the federal budget.

"The people are closely divided in partisan terms but they're united -- two-thirds to 75 percent of them are united -- in what they want us to do," the president said in an interview broadcast Sunday on ABC, telling viewers his top priority was a balanced budget.

Unfortunately voters gave Clinton and the Republicans no roadmap of the way to bridge differences that brought talks to a standstill early this year. So Republicans, independent analysts and even the president's chief of staff worry the talks may dissolve into gridlock as they did 10 months ago after 50 hours of negotiations between Clinton and top Republican leaders, a group that then included Bob Dole.

The two sides tried to agree on a balanced budget plan to end the need for additional borrowing in fiscal 2002. Each annual shortfall between income and spending -- the deficit -- adds to the net national debt, now nearly $3.8 trillion.

Clinton lowered the deficit for each of the past four years. It dipped to $107 billion in the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, the lowest since $79 billion in 1981, but experts projected it will begin rising this fiscal year and continue to go up unless spending is restrained.

Clinton said he was confident all sides could get together, resume talks where they left off and reach an "easily achievable" balanced budget. If agreement is not achieved within a year, however, "it would be difficult to imagine that we could get it," he said.

The president said in the ABC interview, recorded Friday, that he thought an agreement could be reached because the two sides "were so close when we adjourned our budget negotiations ... very, very close in dollar numbers."

But that may not be enough. A senior House Republican staffer said members "are looking through this in a political prism and they don't trust President Clinton. Maybe that will evaporate but we'll have to get further from the election."

During the campaign Clinton accused the Republicans of seeking to cut Medicare to pay for tax cuts for the wealthy. Repubicans say they merely wanted to slow its growth and accused Clinton of "Mediscare."
What Republicans want is for the president to show them a fresh approach that gives them a reason to negotiate.

"The president proposes and the Congress disposes," said California Republican Representative Bill Thomas, who chairs the House Health subcommittee that oversees Medicare. "We're waiting for the president to do what he is supposed to do."
But there is no indication Clinton had anything new to show.

"I'd be shocked if there was a real surprise out there," said Stanley Collender, director of the Federal Budget Consulting Group at Burston-Marsteller. "There really hasn't been a whole lot of policy-making going on for the past six months" while Clinton ran for re-election.

Democrats contend the president need not make a lot of new policy. "There is no mystery here," said White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta in an appearance over the weekend on CBS. "The president has laid down a balanced budget, he laid it down this last year ... it's there."
As for demands by Republicans that Clinton come out with new proposals, Panetta said, that is a "sure recipe for gridlock."
